sections.category: AMD brings native ROCm support to vime, the vLLM project's reinforcement-learning post-training framework, so large-scale RL fine-tuning of open models now runs end-to-end on Instinct MI355X GPUs from a prebuilt container

bullets.body: The vLLM project announced on July 10 that vime, its reinforcement-learning post-training framework, now runs end-to-end on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs through native ROCm support, a port the post credits to AMD contributors working with the vime community. vime splits an RL run into a decoupled pipeline — model training on Megatron, generation and rollout through vLLM, and a data buffer brokering the two — so the same serving engine that became the default for open-model inference now also drives the reward loop. The release ships as a prebuilt Docker container that removes the from-source build which has long gated ROCm adoption, alongside ROCm-specific integrations and validated end-to-end runs. In the published results on Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and the Qwen3-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, throughput held near 4,100 tokens per GPU per second across 100 training steps, the divergence between training and rollout log-probabilities stayed around 0.012, and reward climbed from roughly zero to about 0.5 to 0.6 by step 100 — the numerical-stability and convergence signals a lab checks before trusting non-NVIDIA silicon for post-training. It matters because reinforcement-learning post-training, not pre-training, is where most of this year's frontier gains are being wrung out, and that phase has been almost entirely CUDA-bound; a working MI355X path gives open-model builders a genuine second hardware vendor for their most compute-hungry stage.

citations.label: vLLM Blog - vime + ROCm: End-to-End RL Post-Training on AMD Instinct GPUs

sections.category: Researchers unveil MemGhost, an automated attack that plants persistent false memories in personal AI agents from a single email, hiding the tampering from the user while steering the agent's answers in later sessions

bullets.body: A team from Nanyang Technological University, A*STAR's CFAR, and Johns Hopkins detailed MemGhost, a technique that poisons the long-term memory of a personal AI agent with one crafted email, in a paper posted to arXiv on July 6 and picked up in security coverage on July 13. When an agent that reads its owner's inbox ingests the message, MemGhost induces it to write attacker-chosen "facts" into its persistent memory files, return an innocuous reply that shows nothing happened, and then let those planted facts shape its behavior in later, unrelated conversations. The framework generates its one-shot payload by training an attacker policy with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning against proxies that reward both memory adoption and conversational stealth, and the authors measure it on WhisperBench, a 108-case benchmark that spans fact and preference poisoning over a live IMAP/SMTP email workflow. It succeeded in 87.5% of background-mode runs against the open-source OpenClaw agent on GPT-5.4 and 71.4% against a Claude Code SDK agent on Sonnet 4.6, and it transferred across agent architectures and memory backends. There is no clean patch: OpenClaw's policy treats prompt injection as out of scope unless it crosses an authorization boundary, and the researchers' proposed defenses — tagging the provenance of every stored fact, requiring user approval before a memory write, and logging all memory changes — are architectural changes rather than a switch a user can flip. The result reframes agent memory, usually sold as a convenience feature, as an unaudited persistence layer an outsider can write to.

citations.label: arXiv - When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell: Stealthy Memory Injection in Persistent Personal Agents
The Hacker News - New MemGhost Attack Plants Persistent False Memories in AI Agents Through One Email

sections.category: Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security report finds 99.9% of fixable AI vulnerabilities sitting unpatched, even as most adopters have already pushed agent frameworks and vector databases into production

bullets.body: Orca Security's 2026 State of AI Security report, summarized July 13, found that 99.9% of AI-related vulnerability alerts that already have a fix available remain unpatched — a defensive-posture gap surfacing the same week researchers demonstrated working attacks on agent memory. Drawing on scans of live cloud estates, the report says 81.2% of organizations running AI packages carry at least one known vulnerability and 74.1% carry at least one critical CVE, while between 87% and 98% of organizations across the major clouds have not enabled customer-managed encryption keys for their AI services. The exposure is not confined to research labs: 56% of AI adopters have already deployed agent frameworks into production and 64% operate vector databases wiring language models into internal data, yet nearly 30% store at least one AI API key in an insecure location. Orca's read is that teams are optimizing for deployment speed over fundamentals — patching, key management, encryption — precisely as agentic systems acquire the autonomy and tool access that turn a single unpatched flaw into a self-propagating incident. Placed next to the week's memory-injection and coding-agent disclosures, the report supplies the denominator: the attack techniques are novel, but the surface they land on is overwhelmingly unpatched by default.

citations.label: Help Net Security - 99.9% of fixable AI vulnerabilities remain unpatched (Orca Security 2026 State of AI Security report)

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: AMD Advancing AI opens Moscone on July 22-23, then an August-onward run of chip, security, and developer summits, with World Summit AI newly added to the calendar for Amsterdam in October

bullets.body: The nearest date remains AMD Advancing AI 2026 at San Francisco's Moscone West on July 22-23, where Lisa Su and partners are expected to detail the Instinct MI450 accelerator and Zen 6 EPYC "Venice" CPUs — a fitting counterpoint to this month's AMD-on-vLLM reinforcement-learning work. The AI-chip and infrastructure track behind it runs Hot Chips at Stanford on August 23-25 (the early-registration rate closes July 31) and the AI Infra Summit at the Santa Clara Convention Center on September 15-17. The AI-security track clusters from early August: Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village in Las Vegas on August 1-6, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay on August 11-12, OWASP Global AppSec USA in San Francisco on November 5-6, and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series for teams working agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense. On the developer, data, and Bay Area track, Anyscale's Ray Summit runs August 24-26 at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis, the next AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup lands in August in its usual working-demo format, Ai4 2026 fills The Venetian in Las Vegas on August 4-6, the ACM AI Leadership Summit runs August 30 to September 2 in Atlanta, The AI Conference returns to Pier 48 in San Francisco on September 29 to October 1, GitHub Universe is October 28-29, AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, and NeurIPS 2026 closes the year in December. New on the calendar this week: World Summit AI brings its roughly 10,000-attendee flagship to Amsterdam's Taets Art & Event Park on October 7-8, a practical add for anyone already mapping the European autumn circuit. Near-term actions: register for AMD Advancing AI before the July 22 open, lock the July 31 Hot Chips early rate, and book Black Hat plus the Half Moon Bay AI Risk Summit for the early-August security block.

citations.label: World Summit AI - Amsterdam, Taets Art & Event Park, October 7-8, 2026
